front: State the two named sinuses of the pericardium and their locations.
back: Transverse sinus: behind the aorta and pulmonary artery. Oblique sinus: behind the left atrium.

front: Normal volume of pericardial fluid?
State the 2-D echo definitions of small, moderate, and large pericardial effusion.
back: Small: < 0.5 cm at end-diastole. Moderate: 0.5–2 cm. Large: > 2 cm.

front: What is the MOST SPECIFIC echo sign of cardiac tamponade?
back: Right ventricular diastolic collapse. (Most sensitive: RA inversion > 1/3 of the cardiac cycle.)

front: What respiratory changes in transvalvular flow suggest tamponade?
back: Exaggerated respirophasic variation: > 25% increase in tricuspid inflow with inspiration AND > 25% decrease in mitral inflow with inspiration (opposite pattern from normal).

front: Why does inspiration paradoxically decrease LV filling in constrictive pericarditis?
back: The rigid pericardium prevents the drop in intrathoracic pressure from being transmitted to the LA. So the gradient between pulmonary veins (falling with inspiration) and LA is reduced → less LV filling. Simultaneously RV filling is unchanged/enhanced → septal shift toward LV.

front: State the four 2013 ASE Nagueh criteria for constrictive pericarditis.
back: 1) Respiration-related ventricular septal shift. 2) Preserved or increased medial mitral annular e′ ≥ 9 cm/s. 3) Prominent hepatic vein expiratory diastolic flow reversal (ratio ≥ 0.79). 4) IVC plethora (max diameter ≥ 21 mm and < 50% inspiratory collapse).

front: How is 'annulus reversus' defined and what does it suggest?
back: Medial e′ velocity > lateral e′ velocity (E′_lateral / E′_medial < 1). Suggests constrictive pericarditis — lateral annular motion is restricted by pericardial adhesion/calcification.

front: How is 'annulus paradoxus' defined and what does it suggest?
back: Inverse (rather than positive) correlation between E/e′ and wedge pressure. In CP the medial e′ is paradoxically preserved or exaggerated despite elevated LAP, so E/e′ underestimates filling pressure. Sign of constriction.

front: What e′ velocity cutoff has 95% sensitivity and 96% specificity for constrictive pericarditis?
back: Medial mitral annular e′ > 8 cm/s (using ≥ 9 cm/s in the 2013 ASE criteria).

front: How do you distinguish constrictive pericarditis from restrictive cardiomyopathy on TDI?
back: Constriction preserves relaxation → normal or elevated medial e′ (≥ 9 cm/s). Restriction impairs both relaxation and stiffness → reduced e′ (< 8 cm/s).

front: How does COPD mimic constrictive pericarditis on Doppler and how do you distinguish them?
back: Both can show > 25% respiratory variation in mitral E. In COPD: mitral inflow is NOT restrictive AND there is marked inspiratory INCREASE in SVC forward flow. In CP: SVC forward flow is minimally variable with respiration and mitral inflow is restrictive.

front: Describe cath findings characteristic of constrictive pericarditis.
back: Elevated and equalized RVEDP, LVEDP, and mean RAP (within ~5 mmHg). Rapid y descent. 'Dip-and-plateau' (square-root) sign. PASP < 50 mmHg. DISCORDANT respiratory changes in LV vs RV pressure (opposite direction).

front: How do LV and RV systolic pressures change with respiration in constriction vs restriction?
back: Constriction: DISCORDANT changes (LV and RV pressures move in opposite directions with respiration — ventricular interdependence). Restriction: CONCORDANT changes.

front: State the pericardial thickness threshold and modality for the diagnosis of CP.
back: Pericardial thickness ≥ 3 mm by TEE has 95% sensitivity, 86% specificity. CT and cMRI are also useful. Thickening is not required for the diagnosis — physiology alone can support CP.

front: On M-mode, what is a 'septal bounce' or 'septal shudder' and what does it suggest?
back: Abrupt displacement of the IVS in early diastole caused by RV filling pressure transiently exceeding LV filling pressure. Highly suggestive of constrictive pericarditis. Also seen in massive RV volume overload.

front: What echo findings suggest congenital absence of the left hemipericardium?
back: Enlargement of RV and leftward shift of the heart on standard views; excessive posterior LV wall motion; paradoxical septal motion mimicking RV volume overload (similar appearance to a large ASD).

front: Where do most pericardial cysts occur, and what is their appearance?
back: ~70% at the right cardiophrenic angle. Well-defined, thin-walled, echo-lucent structure without internal echoes. Usually asymptomatic — conservative management.

front: State four common causes of a large pericardial effusion.
back: Malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma, melanoma), uremia, tuberculosis, autoimmune disease (SLE, RA), post-cardiac surgery (Dressler-like syndrome), aortic dissection (hemopericardium), viral pericarditis.

front: When should conservative therapy be tried before pericardiectomy in new constrictive pericarditis?
back: When there is evidence of ongoing inflammation (elevated CRP/ESR or imaging inflammation), the patient is hemodynamically stable, and there are no chronic signs (cachexia, AF, hepatic dysfunction, pericardial calcification). A 3–6 month anti-inflammatory trial is recommended.
